body_markdown:
*John* writes:


Hi Sajeev,


I had a question about ATF. I’ve always understood that ATF does two things: lubricate, but also facilitate friction in the wet clutches, or in the case of a CVT, between the metal belt or chain and pulleys. I don’t really understand the complete role of ATF, but I know that failure to use the correct type can be disastrous.


My wife’s old car, a 2008 Nissan Sentra with a 2.0-liter engine and the notorious Jatco CVT, experienced what I would describe as “slipping.” She got the car new and, a year later, Nissan sent a letter extending the transmission warranty to 10 years / 100,000 miles. The car wasn’t driven a lot, and 10 years came and went. However, it started to slip badly at about 60,000 miles and I was convinced we were looking at an expensive repair. On even a moderate incline, the car would not accelerate and was becoming undrivable. The engine revs would climb with little to no change in forward momentum.


Nissan


Nissan


At that point, I did a fluid change, using a synthetic NS-2 compatible fluid and I was able to replace almost seven quarts. This transformed the driving characteristics of the car and to this day it drives well and shifts smoothly. It now has about 90,000 miles.


My question is about the importance of ATF in modern automatic transmissions, and especially a CVT. Recommended change intervals are typically long, and some manufacturers claim “lifetime” fluid.


To me, a fluid change seems like cheap insurance. Even if you can’t get all the fluid out by simply dropping the pan, you might get 50 percent or more and that would be significant.


*Sajeev* answers:


*( **UPDATE:** This conversation is aimed at vehicles with lower miles, and the need to extend their service life via transmission fluid services. Vehicles with over 100,000 miles may or may not find this information relevant.)*


Your assessment of fluid servicing being “cheap insurance” is precisely my answer. The Jatco JF011E has[five common failure points](https://sunbeltvalvebodies.com/blogs/news/understanding-the-jf011e-cvt-transmission-common-issues-and-how-remanufactured-parts-can-help?srsltid=AfmBOormLX2O_CPPDmDjwpzIq4Kdc9oWwGlmUZWJI0nn6H6Tlz0KojjA#:~:text=Common%20Issues%20with%20the%20JF011E%20CVT%20Transmission) , but several can be attributed to poor maintenance. Confirming the need for fresh transmission fluid is an easy answer, but *Piston Slap* articles are generally known to dig a little deeper. So let’s do just that.


Your question about the “complete role of ATF” needs to be discussed. This oil is unique in the world of automotive lubricants because of its combination of:


- **Viscosity improvers** , for reduced friction at a wide variety of temperatures.
- **Pour point depressants** , which keep fluid flowing in cold weather so the transmission actually shifts when you’re driving.
- **Oxidation inhibitors** , to reduce breakdown in high heat.
- **Anti-foaming agents** , because air bubbles are bad for gearboxes.
- **Corrosion inhibitors** , preventing moisture from corroding metal bits and sensors.
- **Friction modifiers** , adding durability and preventing shudders by some magic of allowing slip when needed, and grabbing when not.
- **Dispersants and detergents** , to keep contamination at bay as sludge and varnish creep into the equation over time.
- **Anti-wear additives.** (This feels self-explanatory.)
- **Extreme pressure additives** , providing a protective film for metal parts when they are experiencing high loads.
- **Dyes** , which ensure you put the right stuff in your gearbox. And if you do not, it’s easy to void a warranty with this color coding.


That’s just a high-level explanation of what comprises transmission fluid, and feel free[to read this website](https://gearsmagazine.com/magazine/the-one-two-threes-of-atfs-part-i/#:~:text=Typical%20additive%20packages%20contain%3A) for more detail. More to the point, these fluids require service over time, even if most automakers would prefer to lower operating costs for most of their customers. There’s also a[carbon footprint](https://earthscience.stackexchange.com/questions/17216/what-is-the-carbon-footprint-of-not-changing-car-oil#:~:text=I%20watched%20the,change%20the%20oil%3F) aspect to consider, but a lack of maintenance still puts a huge financial burden on you down the road, or future owners. But I digress. So let’s revisit this video showing ZF employees telling you to ignore what BMW says about their eight-speed gearboxes.


My mantra these days is to service an automatic gearbox in one of three ways: either every 50-100k miles, or whatever the transmission manufacturer says, ***or*** whatever the “severe” use case says in the automaker’s owner’s manual.


On purpose, this isn’t specific to any vehicle. But since we’re talking Nissans, let’s look at the owner’s manual for a 2018 Nissan Altima, as they have a very odd use case to determine if CVT transmission fluid needs to be serviced.


Nissan


So CVT fluid servicing is only needed if I have stuff on the roof and I use my Altima for glamping?


Most of us would beg to differ, so it comes as no surprise their dealers disagree. A Nissan dealership’s blog[allegedly interviewed their service manager](https://www.nissanoforangepark.com/preowned-nissan-cvt-care-tips-jacksonville-fl/?srsltid=AfmBOoryczWooJURBY0swakfMpz16uyWHilxuoEAKyE1yBBCH9Gfa8hB#:~:text=A%3A%20We,at%20managing%20heat.) , and the unnamed employee reiterated what’s presented here. They suggest CVT-equipped Nissans should have a fluid inspection every 15-30k miles. That’s fair, but that’s also how dealerships get you in the door to upsell you on other services. My three-point suggestion above probably eliminates the need for these inspections, unless you do a lot of muddy-road glamping.


A lot of bang for the buck?


Group 1


So yes, lifetime fluids are likely a complete joke for *Piston Slap* readers. If I had the life of a traveling salesman, I’d even put my money where my mouth is: Nissan Altimas are fantastically respectable rental cars. I enjoy renting them, and I would not hesitate to buy an example with around 40,000 miles, do a CVT service, and drive the absolute heck out of it. My money is on that (theoretical) Altima performing just as well as a similar Toyota Camry or Honda Accord, but it’d save me thousands because of this car’s comparatively worse reputation. Terribly undeserved because of unserviced CVTs, perhaps?


Or not, because *Piston Slap* is a conversation amongst thoughtful folks. So please, tell me what you think in the comments below!
